As we explained at the beginning of this discussion, the Muʿtazilites and Ashʿarites adopted the theory of the indivisible part mainly because of two theological questions: the eternity of the Creator and the created nature of the world, and the problem of how God’s knowledge and power could extend over everything that exists.
In other words, all of them began from the same Islamic intellectual ground.
We can now begin the comparison between al-ʿAllāf’s theory and its Greek source.

From what we have already seen, it is clear that al-ʿAllāf and the other Muʿtazilites influenced by him took only one main element from the atomism of Democritus: the element they could use to prove that the world had been created.
This was the idea that division eventually reaches a final point beyond which an atom can no longer be divided.
For al-ʿAllāf, this meant that matter was finite.
And if matter was finite, then it could not be eternal. It must have come into existence after previously not existing.
Its existence therefore required a cause outside itself.
That cause could not itself have come into existence later. It had to be eternal.
1 — The Atomic Structure of the World According to al-ʿAllāf
Let us now look at how al-ʿAllāf understood the atomic structure of the world, and how he understood atoms themselves.
It is not easy to reconstruct his views with complete confidence, because historians of the Islamic schools have not preserved enough of his own words on this subject.

Al-Shahrastānī, for example, says nothing at all about al-ʿAllāf’s view of the matter. Yet when discussing al-Naẓẓām, he does mention that al-Naẓẓām agreed with the philosophers in rejecting the indivisible part.
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, however, preserves a passage that gives us some idea of al-ʿAllāf’s position.
From al-Ashʿarī’s account, we understand that al-ʿAllāf believed the world to be made up of finite atoms, or indivisible parts.
“The indivisible part has no length, no width, and no depth. It contains neither joining nor separation.”
He also believed that every existing object could be reduced to its final parts, and that the largest number of these smallest parts was eight.
“A mustard seed may be divided into two, then four, then eight, until each of its parts becomes indivisible.”

“A single indivisible substance, when existing by itself, may undergo what bodies undergo in the form of motion and rest, and what results from them”—that is, from motion and rest—“such as joining and separation. But colours, tastes, smells, life, death, and things of this kind cannot exist in the substance. They can exist only in bodies.”
In other words, al-ʿAllāf allowed an individual substance to possess those states whose nature could be understood, but not those whose nature could not.
By this last phrase, al-Ashʿarī means that al-ʿAllāf allowed motion and rest to belong to the individual substance—the indivisible part—because the nature of motion and rest was understood.
But he did not allow colour, taste, smell, life, death, and similar qualities to exist in the substance, or atom, because their nature was not understood. Their true character remained unknown.
Al-Ashʿarī’s statement that joining and separation are produced by motion and rest also suggests that indivisible parts, or atoms, sometimes come together and sometimes move apart.

From this we can conclude that, in Islamic atomism, the compound bodies found in the world are formed when atoms join one another, and dissolve back into their final indivisible parts when those atoms separate.
Bodies therefore come into being through the joining of atoms and pass away through their separation.
On the surface, this seems to fit a theory in which generation and decay take place within nature itself.
But neither the Muʿtazilites nor the Ashʿarites accept the conclusion that would normally follow from this.
All of them reject it, because it directly contradicts the doctrine of divine creation from which they begin.
As for time and space, the logic of motion and rest in al-ʿAllāf’s theory seems to require both.
Time, in fact, would be nothing more than the counting of the successive moments in the motion of atoms, or indivisible parts.
Space would be the field through which those atoms move over time.

Can we therefore conclude that al-ʿAllāf, the Muʿtazilites who followed him, and the other Muslim thinkers who accepted the theory of the indivisible substance—above all the Ashʿarites—also accepted Democritus’s idea of the void?
There is nothing in their surviving statements that clearly shows this.
The words “void” or “empty space” do not appear in the texts transmitted from them.

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, however, one of the major Ashʿarite philosophers, did accept the existence of empty space when discussing the “indivisible substance.” He treated it as the field through which the indivisible part moves.
2 — Comparing al-ʿAllāf’s Theory with the Theory of Democritus
We can now compare the atomism of al-ʿAllāf with that of Democritus and identify where they agree and where they differ.

This comparison will also help us understand the philosophical direction taken by the Muʿtazilites, beginning with al-ʿAllāf, on the structure of the world and on the relationship between this world and Islamic metaphysics as the Muʿtazilites understood it.
We can set out the main conclusions as follows.
A — Al-ʿAllāf, like Democritus, accepts that matter is in motion.
But al-ʿAllāf adds rest alongside motion.
Democritus did not do this, because for him motion belongs inseparably to the existence of atoms.
Al-ʿAllāf may have added rest because both he and the Muʿtazilites as a whole believed that the world had been created, in keeping with the doctrine of divine creation.
If matter—that is, the natural world—came into existence, then motion must also have come into existence.
This means that motion must have an end just as it had a beginning.
And if motion has both a beginning and an end, then it must be preceded by rest and must eventually return to rest.
This helps explain one of al-ʿAllāf’s best-known doctrines, which was unique to him and his followers among Muslim thinkers.

He held that the “movements of the inhabitants of the two eternal abodes” would eventually stop. In other words, even Paradise and Hell in the next world would come to an end as places of continuing motion.

“enter into everlasting stillness and inactivity. In that stillness, all pleasures would be gathered together for the people of Paradise, and all pains would be gathered together for the people of Hell.”
“Just as I do not accept movements that extend infinitely backward, I do not accept movements that extend infinitely forward.”
“It is as though he imagined that what applies to motion does not also apply to rest.”
By this he means that if the doctrine that the world came into existence requires motion to have a beginning and an end, then the same problem should apply to rest as well.
B — Because al-ʿAllāf believed that motion came into existence together with matter, he also held that motion was neither eternal in the past nor everlasting in the future.
Here he differs from Democritus, who regarded motion as eternal and everlasting because of his materialist explanation of the existence of the world.
C — Democritus and al-ʿAllāf agree that bodies are formed when atoms join together and dissolve when atoms separate.
This is their explanation of what Aristotle called “generation and decay.”
But they part company over the final conclusion to be drawn from this theory.

For Democritus, the theory implies that the natural world exists in and through itself. In other words, it removes the need for creation from outside the world and therefore removes the need for a Creator.
Al-ʿAllāf rejects this conclusion because, as a Muslim thinker, he remains committed to divine creation.

So although he explains the formation and dissolution of bodies through atoms joining and separating as they move and come to rest, he explains the existence of the atoms themselves—and the existence of motion and rest within them—through a Creator outside them.
This is the basic point at which Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite atomism separates from the atomism of Democritus.
At this point, the two views take fundamentally different directions.
The Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite view is metaphysical in content and carries an objectively idealist tendency, even though it also contains an early form of dialectical and materialist thinking.
Democritus’s view, by contrast, contains an early materialist and dialectical tendency in both its content and its form.
D — At first sight, Democritus and al-ʿAllāf may appear to agree in the way they describe atoms.
Democritus says that in the void through which atoms move there is no above or below, no middle, no end, and no boundary.
“The indivisible part has no length, no width, and no depth, and contains neither joining nor separation.”
But in reality, the two statements do not agree and are not even talking about the same thing.
Democritus is saying that the void is infinite.
This puts him in direct opposition to al-ʿAllāf, because the infinity of the void is connected, in Democritus’s theory, with the infinity of atoms and the infinity of motion.
The result is an infinite material world.
As we have seen, al-ʿAllāf says the opposite.
His commitment to the created nature of the world means that the world is not eternal in the past and, as a consequence, is not everlasting in the future.
Infinity, by contrast, would imply that the world has no beginning and no end.
When al-ʿAllāf says that the indivisible part has no length, width, depth, joining, or separation, he is describing the nature of the atom itself as something of the greatest possible simplicity.
The two statements therefore do not meet, because they are speaking about different things.
E — Democritus identifies four differences between atoms: shape, size, position, and arrangement.
We find nothing in al-ʿAllāf about these differences or any others of the same kind.
F — The two theories do agree in denying that atoms possess any particular qualitative properties.
Al-ʿAllāf likewise denies that qualities such as colour, taste, smell, life, death, and similar things can exist in the individual substance.
He allows only motion and rest, together with the joining and separation that result from them.
G — Finally, there is the question of change in the natural world.

From everything we have already said about the two theories, it seems that for Democritus—as Aristotle interprets him—the principle of change lies in the changes atoms undergo because of differences in their shape, position, and arrangement, and because their motion brings them together and separates them.
This joining and separation produces combination and dissolution, or “generation and decay.”
These changes come to the atoms from outside their fixed basic nature, or follow from their eternal motion.
They provide the real explanation, and the only causes, for the different phenomena of nature.
Here we find a way to bring together Democritus’s idea that existence does not change at the most basic level with Heraclitus’s idea of generation and becoming.

Bringing these two ideas together also means bringing together the multiplicity of individual things and the unity of existence in a single relationship with a dialectical character: there is no multiplicity without unity.
So Democritus does not absolutely deny change in the natural world.
For al-ʿAllāf, his Muʿtazilite followers, and the Ashʿarites, however, the idea that the world changes is the very foundation on which they build their theory of the indivisible part.
